claim: Average American earned about $1,425 a year, so $1,000 is about eight months' pay
note: Arithmetic on a reported average income.

claim: Dow rose from 63 in August 1921 to 381 in September 1929, about sixfold
About 1.5 million Americans had an account with a broker in 1929, in a population of about 120 million (roughly 1 in 80)
note: Run B, 17 Nov 2026: v2 said 'own any stock at all'. The figure is brokerage customers (Galbraith, citing the Senate count of member-firm accounts), so line 14 was reworded to 'have an account with a broker'. 1 in 80 is arithmetic. UT Austin course text gives the same 1.5 million.

claim: Buyers on margin typically put about 10% down and borrowed the rest
note: The doubling and $10,000 lines are arithmetic on 10% margin.

claim: Many brokers required 40-50% margin by mid-1929
note: Galbraith notes: 'Most brokers required cash of 45% to 50% of the value of the stocks in 1929'. Second source: ryanoconnellfinance.com/1929-stock-market-crash/.

claim: In March 1929 a pool with insider participation pushed RCA ('Radio') stock up over about a week, then sold; pools were not illegal until the Securities Exchange Act of 1934
note: Run B: the v2 wording 'up by almost half in ten days' could not be confirmed (one secondary source; other accounts give roughly 90 to 109). The number was removed and line 23 reworded. NYU paper: pool formed 7 Mar 1929, 'substantial insider participation'. Also https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pool_operation (12 Mar 1929, seven days) and https://sechistorical.org/museum/galleries/kennedy/lastDays_c.php (drove up the price, took gains). The on-screen chart is labelled a sketch, not to scale.

claim: Dow peak close 381.17 on 3 September 1929
Prices fell about 10% in September then rose about 8% by mid-October
Irving Fisher (Yale) said in mid-October 1929 that stock prices had reached what looks like a permanently high plateau
note: Source confirms the Fisher statement, NYT 16 Oct 1929; wording is the widely quoted phrase, used as paraphrase not as a quotation.

claim: Black Thursday 24 Oct 1929: record 12.9 million shares
Bankers bought shares publicly to steady the market; the effort failed
Black Monday 28 Oct: Dow fell nearly 13%
note: The $1,300 line is arithmetic.

claim: Black Tuesday 29 Oct: about 16 million shares, Dow down nearly 12%
note: Percent fall from Federal Reserve History.

claim: Margin calls forced sales as prices fell
By mid-November 1929 the Dow was down almost 50%
Recovery looked imminent to contemporaries in 1930; the decline continued to 1932
note: 'Every rally' is a characterisation.

claim: Dow bottomed 8 July 1932 at 41.22, 89% below the peak
note: $110 is arithmetic on the index, price only.

claim: 1,350 banks suspended in 1930
note: FDIC, The First Fifty Years.

claim: Bank of United States failed 11 Dec 1930 with about $200 million in deposits, then the largest US bank failure
note: historycrunch: 11 Dec 1930, about $200 million, 'then the largest bank failure in United States history', 'an ordinary commercial bank'. Federal Reserve History (banking-panics-1930-31) confirms 11 Dec 1930, New York City.

claim: No federal deposit insurance before 1934; runs converted deposits to cash
note: The lunch-hour scene is an invented illustration of a documented pattern.

claim: About 2,300 banks suspended in 1931
About 9,000 banks suspended operations 1930-1933
note: FDIC First Fifty Years table 3-1 sums to 9,096 for 1930-33. On screen each icon stands for about 225 failed banks (6, then 16, then 40 icons): arithmetic.

claim: Depositors lost about $1.3 billion, 1929-1933
Average prices fell by nearly 30% from 1930 to early 1933
note: $1,400 is arithmetic: 1000 / 0.7.

claim: Unemployment reached about 25% by 1933
Postal Savings: 2% interest, $2,500 cap, depositors quintupled to 2.3 million by 1933
National bank holiday, March 1933
Banking Act signed 16 June 1933 created the FDIC; insurance from 1 Jan 1934 at $2,500
Deposit insurance removes the incentive to run
note: Standard explanation; stated as mechanism.

claim: Dow regained its 1929 high on 23 November 1954
note: Federal Reserve History says November 1954; 23 November 1954 is the standard date of the first close above 381.17.

claim: Insured banks display the FDIC sign
note: FDIC page shows the plaque and seal; 'by the door' is typical, not universal.

claim: Charts drawn on screen (Dow 1921-29, autumn 1929, 1929-32, 1929-54) are sketches of the index's shape; only the labelled figures (63, 381, 41, the dates and the percentages) are claims
note: Intermediate points follow well-known year-end and turning-point levels but are not narrated or labelled.

claim: The on-screen document is titled Banking Act of 1933 and dated 16 June 1933
note: 'President Roosevelt signed the measure, known as the Banking Act of 1933, into law on June 16, 1933.' The president is drawn as a generic figure, not a likeness.
